item.title: 9/11 25 Years Later: A Survivor Remembers
item.description:
Trauma

9/11 25 Years Later: A Survivor Remembers

Reflections on adversity and personal growth by a 9/11 survivor.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Survivors of the 9/11 attack continue to deal with its impact on their lives.
  • Reactions to the attack are varied and complex and range from pathology to personal growth.
  • Personal survivor stories can aid trauma victims in their own recovery journey.

Survivors of the 9/11 attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon have now dealt with their aftereffects for a quarter of a century. Their personal stories are diverse. Some continue to suffer emotionally with trauma and stress-related disorders. Others who were adversely impacted emotionally eventually recovered and now live stable and well-adjusted lives. Some were able to resume their lives with little or no effect on day-to-day adjustment. And others, over time, grew from their experiences on that fateful day.

Four Trajectories Following Trauma

These four outcomes—pathology, resilience, invulnerability, and personal growth—are common responses to adversity and trauma.[1] By necessity, mental health professionals focus on understanding and treating pathologies such as post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, and depression. It is worth noting, however, that trauma survivors, especially over time, may experience multiple trajectories. With treatment and social support, pathology may be followed by resilience or even personal growth. It is unwise and unfair to categorize anyone’s response to trauma with a single label. The human response to major trauma is complicated and highly personal.

Source: Department of War / Air Force Tech. Sgt. Cedric H. Rudisill (public domain)

A 9/11 Survivor’s Personal Story

Army Lieutenant Colonel Marilyn Wills, a survivor of the Pentagon attack, was working in the section of the Pentagon struck by American Airlines Flight 77. In the chaos that followed, she was able to escape through a second-floor window when Commander Craig Powell, a Navy SEAL assigned to the Pentagon, caught her in a fall. Although she bravely assisted others in evacuating the building, many of her colleagues did not survive the attack.[2]

In the recent National Geographic documentary series 9/11: Reunited, Col. Wills and Cmdr. Powell were reunited for the first time since the attack.[3] Sharing their memories of that day, 25 years later, was part of the long healing process. After viewing the documentary, I had the honor of interviewing Col. Wills about her long journey to recovery. What follows are insights she shared.

In our conversation, we discussed the trajectory of Col. Wills’ recovery journey. She related that she faced major struggles in the months and years following the attack. Although highly motivated to continue her Army career, she found that her chain of command showed little empathy for her traumatic experience, telling her to “soldier up” and do her job. Col. Wills reported she did not get much professional help in coming to terms with her trauma. “I think I may have seen a psychiatrist once. The chaplain may have come by once or twice, and that was it.” In retrospect, she firmly believes that regular mental health support would have speeded her recovery. “That would have helped move me forward quicker than I did. Honestly, I had no growth. I was surviving. I was treading water.”

For years, Col. Wills was reluctant to speak with anyone, even her family, about the attack. Moreover, she experienced survivor’s guilt. “In my mind, I had a difficult time understanding why I am still here. And that person is not. That person that was right next to me,” she stated. “I wouldn't even talk about 9/11 for five to seven years.” Now, 25 years later, she can speak openly about her experiences. She says that she has turned her attention outward, away from herself, and more toward others. Family and friends provide social support integral to resilience. “At some point something flipped, and I thought, how can I be externally focused and help others, which was the best therapy of all.”

Drawing on strengths of character helped Col. Wills’ recovery. In the immediate aftermath of 9/11, she mentions several character strengths that helped her cope. “In the days following the attack, the character strength most helpful to me was my spirituality.” She also emphasized that the character strength of courage was of significant importance to her at that time. “I had courage, but I didn't know because I hadn't been tested. We go one day forward, that's when that courage came in to say you can do this.”

Another character strength instrumental in her recovery was forgiveness. For Col. Wills, forgiveness did not come easily at first but was something that developed over time. “I had to ask myself for forgiveness for continuing to live my life, because in my mind, I kept asking, why am I here? Why? Forgiveness was huge for me. And it was a lot I had to work through with that.”

As time passed, courage and the character strengths of humanity—caring for others, kindness, and positive social relationships—played integral roles in her adjustment. Col. Wills firmly believes that, over time, she has become resilient. “I knew I had to bounce back from this tragedy. And the question was, how are you going to do this, Marilyn? What steps are you going to take? What is that going to look like for you? And I think resilience was there all along. It was latent, but that has been there and is my whole thing. And every day I try something new.”

Col. Wills’ response to 9/11 illustrates the complexity of response to trauma. Her mental health was challenged but, over time, her pathology trajectory changed into one of resilience and growth. Hers was not a single trajectory, but several spread over time.

Finally, Col. Wills reflected on advice to others who have experienced trauma. “I would share the following with those victims. First, acknowledge that it did happen, and now how do you move forward? Continue to add tools in your bag to help you move forward. Don’t minimize the event. You had been moving forward in life. Now, reflect back and remember those things that helped you move forward and bring those back to the surface. Finally, bring back those latent character strengths.”

An Object Lesson for Trauma Survivors

As we commemorate the 25th anniversary of 9/11, it is important to remember people like Col. Wills. Because many of us will experience a traumatic event in our lives,[4] Col. Wills’ story provides an object lesson in what we may expect. Adverse psychological reactions may likely occur. But by actively seeking therapy, embracing the social support of family and friends, and harnessing character strengths to build perspective and meaning, more positive trajectories are likely.

Note: The views expressed herein are those of the author and do not reflect the position of the United States Military Academy, the Department of the Army, or the Department of Defense.

item.title: Does Melatonin Raise the Risk of Heart Failure?
item.description:
Psychopharmacology

Does Melatonin Raise the Risk of Heart Failure?

What the latest evidence says about melatonin and cardiovascular health.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • An AHA abstract linked long-term recorded melatonin use to a higher heart failure risk.
  • The observational design cannot establish that melatonin caused the increased risk.
  • Insomnia itself can affect cardiovascular health and complicate the findings.
  • Randomized trials have reported some encouraging cardiovascular effects of melatonin.
Source: Robina Weermeijer / Unsplash

Melatonin is widely used as a sleep aid, with its regulatory status varying between countries. That made a conference abstract presented at the American Heart Association’s 2025 Scientific Sessions particularly alarming. The researchers reported that adults with insomnia whose medical records indicated at least a year of melatonin use had an 89 percent higher hazard of developing heart failure over the following five years.

The abstract analyzed 130,828 adults with insomnia using electronic health records from the TriNetX Global Research Network. Half had at least 365 days of recorded melatonin exposure, while the other half had no melatonin exposure recorded. Heart failure occurred in 4.6 percent of the melatonin group compared with 2.7 percent of the comparison group. The researchers also reported higher rates of heart failure hospitalization and death from any cause among people with recorded melatonin use.

The numbers are striking, but because the analysis was observational, they cannot establish that melatonin caused the higher rate of heart failure. The findings also raise questions about how accurately the recorded exposure reflects actual melatonin use and whether the two groups differed in ways that the researchers could not account for.

What the abstract could not tell us

The researchers matched the two groups across numerous characteristics, including medical conditions, medications, laboratory results, vital signs, and health care use. This can reduce differences between the groups, but it cannot account for information that was never recorded.

The analysis identified melatonin exposure through prescription and other recorded data. That means it could not show whether participants actually took the melatonin, and the abstract does not give enough detail about dose or how consistently it was used.

The TriNetX database uses health records from different countries, where melatonin is not accessed in the same way. In the United States, it is available without a prescription, while in the United Kingdom it is prescription-only. A person taking melatonin in the U.S. could therefore have no prescription record at all, meaning that some actual users may have been classified as having no recorded exposure.

All of the participants had insomnia, which is itself associated with cardiovascular problems, including heart failure.

Insomnia already has cardiovascular consequences

Chronic insomnia can affect the cardiovascular system in several ways. Persistent sleep disruption can keep the body in a state of heightened stress, with increased sympathetic nervous system activity, higher blood pressure, and changes in the hormones involved in the stress response.

Over time, these effects can place additional strain on the heart and blood vessels and contribute to cardiovascular disease, including heart failure. The longer sleep problems persist, the more relevant this cumulative effect may become.

Cardiovascular disease can also interfere with sleep. Symptoms and physiological changes associated with cardiovascular problems can disrupt normal sleep, sometimes before the condition has been diagnosed. This means that insomnia can precede cardiovascular disease, follow it, or develop alongside it.

The finding does not fit neatly with other cardiovascular research

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis examined four randomized trials involving patients with heart failure. Although the evidence was limited, the authors reported improvements in quality of life, NT-proBNP, and some measures of cardiac function, and concluded that melatonin might have a role as an adjunctive treatment for heart failure.

An even broader systematic review published in 2026 included 14 randomized trials and 1,027 participants with cardiovascular disease. Melatonin was associated with a significant improvement in the change in left ventricular ejection fraction, particularly among patients undergoing coronary artery bypass surgery. The results were not consistently positive across all cardiovascular outcomes, however, and the authors emphasized substantial differences between the trials.

The results were encouraging, particularly because some of the trials involved people who already had heart failure. Although the evidence is not yet definitive, the findings raise the possibility that melatonin could have beneficial cardiovascular effects, which is difficult to reconcile with the idea that it substantially increases the risk of heart failure.

What should melatonin users make of this?

The AHA abstract does not provide enough evidence to conclude that melatonin causes heart failure. However, its findings raise a legitimate question about long-term use that deserves further investigation, particularly in research that can measure dose, duration, and actual exposure more accurately.

For people taking melatonin, the findings are also a reason to pay attention to the insomnia being treated. Persistent insomnia has itself been associated with cardiovascular problems, so treating sleep difficulties should not be reduced to taking a sleep aid. If insomnia continues over time, it may be worth discussing other approaches with a health professional rather than relying indefinitely on melatonin.

Clinicians may also want to ask specifically about melatonin when reviewing a patient's medications and supplements. People do not always mention it because they may think of it as a supplement rather than a medication, and its use may therefore be absent from the medical record.

For now, the 2025 abstract is best viewed as a signal that warrants further research, not as evidence that melatonin increases the risk of heart failure. The available cardiovascular research, including randomized trials in people with heart disease, does not point in a single direction of harm. That makes the question of long-term melatonin use worth investigating without turning one preliminary finding into a reason for alarm.

item.title: Is Your GLP-1 Drug Making You Sleepy or Exhausted?
item.description:
Sleep

Is Your GLP-1 Drug Making You Sleepy or Exhausted?

GLP-1 medications can cause fatigue, exhaustion, and sleepiness.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • GLP-1 drugs affect more than appetite for food: They can make you feel tired, sleepy, or exhausted.
  • Fatigue is the second most common complaint after gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea).
  • A social media platform analysis revealed that 14% to 16% of people on GLP-1 medications report fatigue.
  • People who are taking GLP-1 drugs should be monitored for correctable causes of fatigue.
Source: KaterynaBorodina/Shutterstock

If you’re taking a glucagon-like peptide receptor agonist (GLP-1 or GLP-1 RA) for weight loss, obesity, diabetes, or sleep apnea, you may have noticed that you feel sleepy, even exhausted, for the first couple of days after your injection as you’re ramping up the dose.

I’ve been taking GLP-1 RA injections for several months, gradually increasing the dose, and lost 23 pounds. I felt great and energized, and had no side effects until I reached the highest dose. Then it hit me.

Source: PeopleImages/Shutterstock

On the day after my injection and through the following day, I could barely get off the couch. I slept 12 hours, managed to go out for a short time, and then promptly fell asleep in my recliner for over an hour. It was all I could do to stay awake until 8:30 p.m. and then head back to bed for more sleep. Then, as suddenly as it had started, I perked up 48 hours after my dose, with my usual level of energy. I swam for 30 minutes before breakfast after seven hours of sleep.

In the depths of exhaustion, I began to wonder if I had chronic fatigue syndrome, and for the first time truly understood what patients with that debilitating disorder experience. But it turns out that fatigue is a known side effect of GLP-1 RAs. The problem is that fatigue has multiple definitions, and many clinical trials don’t specifically call out the different ways that people define fatigue: sleepiness, “weak and dizzy,” exhaustion.

It is fascinating that a drug that targets the brain’s dopamine reward pathways to reduce appetite can have such massive effects on fatigue and sleepiness.

In my case, there was the additional complicating factor of my thyroid gland, that butterfly-shaped gland in your neck that makes thyroid hormone, which revs up your metabolism. People with thyroid conditions in which the hormone is low gain weight and feel sleepy and exhausted. That’s how my hypothyroidism was diagnosed 25 years ago—I would fall asleep on the couch at 7 p.m. I put the fatigue down to stress, but in fact, I had developed an autoimmune disease called Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, which scars the thyroid gland that produces that vital hormone. Low thyroid is one of the most treatable illnesses in medicine, because thyroid hormone pills are readily available to replace what your glands can’t make. It seems that the GLP-1 RA or my weight loss interfered with the dose of the hormone I was taking. But bumping up the dose didn’t stop the exhaustion I felt for 48 hours after each injection.

So, what is the evidence that GLP-1 RAs cause fatigue and how do they do it?

While fatigue hasn’t reached reporting thresholds in most clinical trials, a 2026 Nature Health study analyzing self-reported side effects on the social media platform Reddit found that after nausea and gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue was the most common complaint, with 16.7 percent of over 67,000 GLP-1 RA users complaining of fatigue. The percentage of those complaining of fatigue was similar for semaglutide (16.1 percent) and tirzepatide (14.7 percent). A 2025 randomized clinical trial reported in the New England Journal of Medicine found that 11.3 percent of 750 participants reported fatigue but emphasized that the most common side effects were gastrointestinal. A 2021 clinical trial published in the Journal of the American Medical Association reported 7.3 percent of participants complaining of fatigue.

Fatigue has many causes, including dehydration, which can result from diarrhea and vomiting. But in my case, I had no GI side effects, and I wasn’t dehydrated. Sleep disruption is another cause. But my smart ring told me that my sleep was not disrupted. In fact, with my reduced weight, my sleep apnea had improved.

Other causes of fatigue include anemia, low iron, and low blood sugar, all of which could occur in people with gastrointestinal side effects with reduced absorption of essential nutrients. But I had none of those.

Dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, with low cortisol, has been reported in chronic fatigue syndrome. GLP-1 RAs can also affect mood, and mood disorders are also associated with fatigue. Because GLP-1 RAs target receptors in the hypothalamus and in the brain's feel-good dopamine reward pathways, one wonders if those brain regions and pathways might contribute to fatigue.

Finally, low blood pressure can cause weakness and fatigue, so as you lose weight, the dose of your blood pressure meds may need to be adjusted.

Compared to some of the more severe side effects, such as pancreatitis and gallbladder disease, nausea, diarrhea, and vomiting, fatigue may seem like a minor complaint. And while 7 percent to 16 percent may not seem like much, when you are one of those people, it’s 100 percent, and it can totally throw you off your game and interfere with your quality of life.

It helps to know that the fatigue only lasts a couple of days and diminishes as you get used to the new dose. So, if you can ride it out, the benefits of the weight loss and correction of sleep apnea, sugar metabolism, diabetes, and its associated cardiovascular risks are well worth it. But now that I’ve experienced this debilitating side effect, I believe that more clinical trials should include more granular questions addressing the many ways in which people define fatigue so that its causes can be identified and addressed. Staying hydrated, eating a well-balanced diet, and treating any of the many potential causes of fatigue should also be part of the regimen for anyone on GLP-1 RAs who experiences fatigue.

item.title: Hormones, Hardship, or Mental Illness?
item.description:
Health

Hormones, Hardship, or Mental Illness?

Context matters: Looking beyond psychiatric labels in women's mental healthcare.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Hormonal transitions, stress, and psychiatric disorders can produce similar symptoms.
  • Understanding when symptoms occur and what influences them can help to identify appropriate care.
  • Hormones, stress, and mood disorders can overlap; comprehensive assessment is essential.

Imagine sitting in an overly heated room, only to be told you have a fever. Though your body temperature is undeniably up, you might question your "fever" label if paracetamol won’t help.

Women navigating the mental healthcare system can face a similar dilemma when symptoms relating less to psychiatric illness and more to hormonal shifts, external stressors, or both are attributed to primary anxiety or depressive disorders.

A two-pronged blind spot can arise in clinical practice, where different contributing factors can be overlooked or misattributed in the assessment of women's symptoms:

  • External structural pressures: domestic violence, gendered expectations around invisible household labour, insecure work, and lifelong pay and superannuation gaps can leave women bearing significant psychological tolls.
  • Internal physiological transitions: hormonal shifts across the menstrual cycle, perimenopause, and the postpartum period can influence mood and anxiety, sometimes producing severe or episodic symptoms.

Research shows that antidepressant prescribing can be 40 percent higher among women than men, with prescribing also varying by age and socioeconomic circumstances. This does not demonstrate inappropriate treatment, but it does raise an important question about whether prescribing decisions always account for the full biological, psychological, and social context of women's mental health. Symptoms alone don’t point to cause.

The argument doesn’t strike at diagnosis, medication, or psychiatric care. Used appropriately, diagnosis opens the door to effective treatment, which substantially improves quality of life. The question is whether consumers of healthcare and the industry itself can overvalue diagnoses when more questions should be asked about women’s symptoms and whether they are best understood using psychiatric labels.

A Women’s "If-Then" Guide to Understanding Anxiety and Depression

There is no single cause of anxiety or depression. Biology, psychology, and circumstances interact, and symptoms alone rarely tell us which factors matter most.

A useful starting point is to ask not just what do you feel, but when do you feel the way you do, and what happens to your feelings when your specific circumstances change.

1. The Hormonal Check: The Luteal Neurosteroid Paradox

If low mood, despair, anxiety, or rage appear predictably during the luteal phase of your menstrual cycle (two to one week(s) before menstruation) and disappear within days of menstruation beginning, then hormonal sensitivity may contribute to your problems.

Reproductive mood symptoms are not simply due to having “too much” or “too little” estrogen or progesterone. Perimenopausal and postnatal hormonal changes can influence anxiety and mood in complex ways. Premenstrual dysphoric disorder seems to involve heightened sensitivity to normal hormonal fluctuations.

It is important to assess the pattern of your symptoms. If anxiety or mood symptoms appear and disappear reliably, syncing with hormonal cycles, that pattern tells you more about your issue than the symptoms themselves. The predictability of your symptoms can inform the diagnostic picture and, in turn, the most appropriate treatment.

2. The Situational Check: The Biopsychosocial Stress Load

If anxiety or low mood improves substantially when you experience genuine relief from an overwhelming situation, then your feelings might be highly related to stress.

Chronic financial pressure, excessive workloads, caring responsibilities, relationship conflict, or unsafe environments can contribute to a prolonged state of hypervigilance. Over time, this can affect sleep, concentration, mood, energy, and emotional regulation.

Anxiety and depression arising in response to hardship are genuine and warrant attention. Having a reaction to an obvious stressor does not necessarily mean you have a psychiatric disorder. Still, it does not rule one out. The effects of prolonged stress can persist long after your circumstances improve, and you may require further investigation.

3. The Depression Check: When Symptoms Persist

If low mood, anxiety, or loss of interest does not follow a predictable hormonal pattern, and continues even when your circumstances improve significantly, then you may be experiencing what is known to be a primary anxiety or depressive disorder.

A primary anxiety or depressive disorder is not simply a chemical imbalance. Clinical anxiety and depression emerge from the interaction of biological vulnerabilities, psychological processes, and life circumstances. Triggers might be apparent; sometimes they aren’t. The persistence of symptoms can be an important clue to your presentation. That said, persistence alone does not determine a psychiatric diagnosis.

A Comprehensive Approach Is Essential

Hormones, stressful circumstances, and psychiatric conditions are not mutually exclusive. Women can be hormonally sensitive, chronically overwhelmed, and clinically depressed at the same time.

Considering all possible contributors to the way you feel is important to ensure your feelings are assessed comprehensively and you receive the most suitable support or treatment that is available.

Sometimes a fever needs paracetamol. Sometimes you could do with a cooler room.

item.title: "The Odyssey": How an Ancient Epic Created a Cultural Moment
item.description:
Complex PTSD

"The Odyssey": How an Ancient Epic Created a Cultural Moment

Within each of us lies a sleeping hero, waiting to be awakened.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Odysseus is not a perfect hero, he is flawed; he represents the sleeping hero in all of us.
  • The essence and energy of every mythic archetype is intricately woven into our psyche.
  • The word "psyche" in Greek means “soul,” forming the root of the word "psychology" (“the study of the soul”).

In the age of reality distortion, parasocial relationships, and increased use of AI, we are all craving what is real, what is true, and what is familiar. Christopher Nolan’s new adaptation of The Odyssey has sparked a renewed global obsession with Greek mythology. You may wonder how stories from thousands of years ago still endure and resonate so powerfully today. The power of The Odyssey lies in its simplicity. Odysseus is not a perfect or moral hero; he is flawed, he is learning, he is growing, he is becoming. He represents the sleeping hero in all of us, waiting to be awoken.

While in ancient myth the hero had to slay a monster, in real life, our quest is to conquer the struggles that lie within. Every emotional challenge we face is actually a compelling invitation for growth and self-evolution. The truth is, you will never truly know your own strength, or the true quality of your relationships, until you have been tested by adversity. Think of pain as the elixir the soul drinks to grow and evolve. In the vast tapestry of mythological tales, where gods, mortals, and other creatures play out the timeless dramas of existence, we must remember that the archetypal energy of each mythological figure lives within us, reminding us of the hidden power, resilience, and wisdom that already reside within, waiting to be rediscovered and claimed. (Take the Quiz + Find Out Which Greek Myth Archetype You Are).

Source: Zeeshaan Shabbir / Used with Permission

Despite their ancient origins, the figures from Greek mythology are intricately woven into our contemporary understanding of psychology and the human mind. In fact, many of the terms we use today to map out our mental health—from our darkest phobias (Phobos) to the traps of egocentricism (Narcissus)—trace their roots directly back to the ancient characters in Greek myth.

Sigmund Freud used the myth of Narcissus to describe an overly egocentric, self-loving character whose libido focuses on the self. Today, this term has developed into a formal diagnosis (narcissistic personality disorder). Narcissus was a proud young hunter renowned and celebrated for his beauty. He had many admirers; however, he chose to remain alone. By rejecting all romantic advances, he broke many hearts. The myth of Narcissus is a cautionary tale warning against the perils of vanity and self-adoration. Despite his captivating appearance, his arrogance, self-focused energy, and inflated self-importance alienated Narcissus from his peers and led him to a life of isolation. Narcissus represents the tragic nexus between the power of beauty and the pain of superiority.

Source: Zeehaan Shabbir/ Used with Permission

In the realm of Greek mythology, Phobos stands as the very essence of fear, a haunting presence that instills dread in the hearts of mortals. The son of Ares, the god of war, and Aphrodite, the goddess of love and beauty, Phobos often accompanied his father into battle. Phobos struck terror into the hearts of enemy soldiers and civilians, paralyzing them by amplifying the chaos and danger of war in their mind. His harrowing appearance, often portrayed as a boy with a lion’s head, was a common emblem embossed on the shields of gods and mortals seeking to harness his power and strike fear into the hearts of their enemies. Heroes of such caliber as Hercules and Achilles integrated his image into their armory, as the mere sight of Phobos’s likeness had the power to invoke sensations of terror, panic, and petrification. Phobos reigns as a potent figure, a reminder of the fears that lurk within the human soul. And in time, he became the inspiration behind the word phobia.

While some archetypes represent our darkness, others represent our light. The essence and energy of every mythic archetype is intricately woven into our psyche, shaping our thoughts, behaviors, and experiences as we move through life. These universal and timeless stories shape our understanding of life, adversity, what it means to be human, and—perhaps most importantly—love. The enduring power of myths lies in their ability to reconnect us to something larger than ourselves, inspiring us to live more meaningful and compassionate lives and, most importantly, reminding us of our natural inclination toward doing good. One of the most captivating stories of love in Greek mythology is that of Psyche and Eros. Psyche, the Goddess of the Soul, goes through trials and tribulations to be reunited with Eros, the God of Love. Their story symbolizes the soul’s journey of overcoming trials, aligning with love, and transforming through growth. In life, we are all on a journey toward sacred reunion, a process of integrating love with the soul.

Even the origin of the word psychology leads us back to myth; the word psyche in Greek means “soul,” forming the root of words like psychology (“the study of the soul”) and psychiatry (“the healing of the soul”). And so you have it, Greek myth has been hidden in plain sight all along, used in our vernacular and informing our world in ways big and small. Ancient wisdom, passed down from generation to generation through storytelling, eventually becomes regarded as myth and legend. The practical wisdom of the collective unconscious is not to be disregarded but revered as the language of the soul. Myths are more than mere stories; the archetypes within them serve as mirrors and maps, reminding you of the power, resilience, and wisdom that reside within you, waiting to be rediscovered and claimed.

item.title: How to Take a Joywalk for Your Mental Health
item.description:
Mindfulness

How to Take a Joywalk for Your Mental Health

Author John Schu on the joy of walking with mindfulness and gratitude.

Posted September 10, 2026

Author John Schu shares the story of joywalking in his latest picture book, Lily-May’s Joyful Day, and encourages readers of all ages to find joy in taking a walk with a grateful heart.
Source: Penguin Random House/Used with permission

We’ve all heard the advice that it's good to take a walk for your mental health, but what about taking a joywalk?

Walking releases endorphins, hormones that decrease stress and promote happiness, and going for walks regularly has even been shown to reduce symptoms of clinical anxiety and depression (Xu et al., 2024).

For librarian, educator, and children’s book author John Schu, walking becomes joyful when combined with two other well-studied mental health practices—mindfulness and gratitude. Together, they form the practice of joywalking.

Schu shares the story of joywalking in his latest picture book, Lily-May’s Joyful Day, and encourages readers of all ages to find joy in taking a walk with a grateful heart.

Q: In your book, Lily-May introduces the concept of joywalking to her classmates. What is a joywalk, and how can families benefit from this practice? How might joywalking promote better mental health for children?

John Schu: I’ve been trying to write a story about joywalking since 2017, but every attempt turned into a different story. I realized I was trying too hard. I was forcing the idea instead of letting the story find me and talk to me in an authentic way.

I finally “cracked the code” during a joywalk in New York City, when I walked past the Bethesda Fountain in Central Park. At the top of the fountain sits the Angel of the Waters, an angel who inspires, comforts, and somehow always helps me open up, as two-time Newbery Medalist Kate DiCamillo would say, “the suitcase of my heart.”

I sat down near the angel, opened my notebook, and wrote these guiding words for my joywalking story:

A joywalk is a time
to listen,
to think,
to wander and roam,
to explore ideas,
and, most importantly,
to notice.

To notice small details.
To notice BIG details.
To reflect on the day.

That became the heart and soul of Lily-May’s Joyful Day.

A joywalk isn’t simply a walk. It’s an invitation to slow down, pay attention, and make space for curiosity and reflection. Families can benefit from practicing joywalking together because it gives them a simple way to step away from the noise and busyness of everyday life and reconnect with themselves, with one another, and with the world around them.

I think that act of noticing can be pretty powerful for children. Joywalking encourages us to pause and become present: to notice something beautiful, to wonder about something we see, to reflect on how we’re feeling, or simply to enjoy the experience of being outside. Those small moments of mindfulness can help us develop tools for managing stress and processing emotions.

In many ways, the Angel of the Waters helped me figure out how to write this story, just as she did when I was writing Louder Than Hunger, my verse novel about anorexia nervosa, obsessive-compulsive disorder, anxiety, depression, and the work it takes to muffle a loud negative voice. Both books, in very different ways, are about what happens when we learn to listen...to ourselves, to the world around us, and to the voices that can help guide us toward something healthier.

On Lily-May’s Joyful Day’s book birthday, Dr. Paul Mullen, a clinical child psychologist and associate professor of psychology at North Central College in Naperville, Illinois, posted, “Happy book birthday to Lily-May’s Joyful Day. Joy grows from mindfulness and gratitude."

That is what I hope joywalking can help children connect with: the understanding that joy doesn’t always have to be something we chase. Sometimes, it begins with slowing down, looking around, and noticing what is already there.

I love Lily-May, and I hope children do, too!

Q: How does reading picture books together help children learn about feelings and mental wellness?

JS: I love picture books. I collect them. I share them. I write them. Our students are never too old to be read a picture book aloud. Or to read one aloud themselves.

Too often, as young readers move toward the upper grades, they’re discouraged from checking out and reading picture books. This is both unfortunate and ironic because this is the exact same time when they can finally read them independently.

Picture books give children a safe and accessible way to explore big feelings, recognize their own experiences in the lives of characters, and begin conversations about mental wellness that might otherwise feel difficult to start. When we read them together, we’re not only sharing a story, we’re giving children language for their emotions and reminding them that they are not alone. And that’s a beautiful thing, isn’t it?

Source: Penguin Random House/Used with permission

Q: What do you hope readers take away from spending time with Lily-May’s Joyful Day?

JS: My hope is that Lily-May’s Joyful Day finds its way into classrooms, libraries, and homes. I hope it finds its way into the hearts and lives of children. I hope it inspires children to create Bags of Y-O-U, take joywalks, notice the little things that bring them joy, and share what inspires them. Most of all, I hope readers come away knowing that joy is something they can discover, nurture, and share.

item.title: Who Is Training Your Character?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Who Is Training Your Character?

Confucius saw habit as self-transformation. Your AI calls it engagement.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Confucius taught us that repeated conduct makes the person.
  • Social media and AI are also systems of repeated conduct, but they were designed by someone else.
  • We can take the training back, one repetition at a time.
Source: Natalia Dobrovolska / Adobe Stock

A few weeks ago, someone took our work. He posted it on social media as if it were his own: no attribution, no acknowledgment, not even a nod in the comments. Naturally, I was furious. And within 20 minutes, I had written a post naming him and laying out exactly what he’d done.

Thirty years ago, I would have published immediately. But time has taught me a few things, so I gave it an hour. And sure enough, by the end of the hour I had written a second version. Same facts, but a much calmer tone, and instead of posting it, I sent it to him privately. He didn’t apologize or withdraw it; instead, he doubled down and continued on his merry plagiarizing way.

I moved on—some people are simply not worth engaging with. But it left me with a question: Which version was the real me? The angry post felt more alive. The second version felt like a compromise, maybe even a small act of cowardice, the kind of thing you do because you have a reputation to manage.

I’ve come to think that’s the wrong question. Both versions were me. The question that matters is, what was I training myself to become?

What Confucius Knew About Manners

One description of what I did is that I censored myself. I had a real reaction, and I edited it for public consumption. That’s how our culture tends to read moments like this: The angry post is the real person, and the polite message is the costume he puts on before going outside.

Confucius saw it very differently. In the Confucian tradition, manners are not merely a set of rules that stop us from behaving badly. They are the path to self-transformation, because repeated appropriate conduct changes the person performing it. The later Confucian thinker Xunzi put it vividly: Human nature is like crooked wood, and ritual is the steaming and pressing that makes it straight. Left to our impulses, we stay bent. Practiced conduct is what gives us shape.

By this light, my private message wasn’t a suppression of character. It was an exercise of it. I wanted to be the kind of person who gives someone a chance to explain before I hold them up for public judgment. The only way to be that person is to do that thing, especially when I don’t feel like it.

The insight is simple: We become what we repeatedly do.

The Machines Are Running Rituals Too

Confucius assumed the ritual was designed by wise people for the benefit of the person performing it. That assumption does not hold in the digital world in which we spend so much of our time. For instance, while social media is also a system of repeated conduct, its rituals were designed by companies rather than by sages, and they point you toward actions that benefit the bottom line rather than anything that helps you grow as a person.

The same holds true of AI. Last year OpenAI had to withdraw an update to ChatGPT because it had become so flattering that users were posting screenshots of it applauding plainly terrible ideas. That was an extreme case, but researchers have found that the tendency to agree with the user runs through every major assistant, because the systems are trained on human approval and humans approve of being agreed with.

So consider the conduct being repeated. Hundreds of times a day, you say something, and something answers that you are right. It never takes offense. It never asks you to phrase anything for the sake of another mind. Confucian ritual exists because human beings are social animals that need to train themselves to get along with other animals; the AI chatbot is a society with no one in it but you, and a machine that is designed to flatter you.

If Confucius is right, then social media and AI are training us to become particular kinds of people. Social media rewards the person who publishes the first draft: quick, certain, and performing for an audience rather than speaking to a person. It rewards extremes, because the measured view earns nothing and the outrageous one travels, so over time it produces polarizers rather than consensus-seekers. Sycophantic AI, meanwhile, produces a person who experiences disagreement as a malfunction, and who eventually stops growing because of it.

But there is hope, and it lies in a simple idea: We need to take the training back. The hour I gave myself before sending that message was proof that the training is contestable. The platform wanted the first draft and did not get it.

Instead of letting social media and AI decide what kind of people we become, we can choose for ourselves, one repetition at a time.

Taking the Training Back

Here are four things you can do today to put your development back into your own hands.

  1. Write the whole thing, then wait an hour. Don’t suppress the first draft. Put every word of it down. Then do nothing with it for 60 minutes.
  2. Notice what the platform is rewarding, then do the other thing. If the design pays you for speed, be slow. If it pays you for certainty, ask a question. Treat the reward as a signal of what you’re being trained toward.
  3. Make the machine disagree with you. Before you accept an AI’s praise, ask it for the strongest case against what you just said. Keep another mind in the room, even an artificial one.
  4. Ask what you’re rehearsing. Before you act, ask: If I did this a hundred times, who would I be? That question tends to answer itself.

The Self You Practice

Both thoughts happened. The fury was real and so was the decision to wait. But the self isn’t found in the first reaction or the second. It lives in the pattern of choices between them, made again and again until they stop feeling like choices and start feeling like character.

The machines are happy to make those choices for us. But it would be wise to make them ourselves.

item.title: How to Parent an Adult Child With Schizophrenia
item.description:
Parenting

How to Parent an Adult Child With Schizophrenia

Advice from a father on parenting an adult with a complex diagnosis.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • It is possible for adults with a schizophrenia diagnosis to lead fulfilling lives.
  • Parenting strategies can go a long way to help make that happen.
  • Being patient, caring, and supportive is key while maintaining realistic assertiveness.
  • Reduce internalized stigma in yourself so that you can support your child.

I’ve lived with a psychotic disorder for 10 years now, and I wouldn’t be here without the devoted support of my father. He has been one of the few people who can bring out my true self while also accepting my psychotic symptoms as part of my whole person. He has been kind yet assertive when reminding me of the reality that I live in. As a result of our recovery “teamwork,” I have accomplished a lot. I got two master’s degrees, live in New York City, and am now a writer.

Recently, people have been very curious about how best to support their child with a schizophrenia diagnosis. I decided to interview my father so that he can share his wisdom for himself.

Jim Myers is a father and sibling of three family members who lived and live with a schizophrenia disorder. He has been my mental health advocate for 20 years. He has often told me that his childhood experience with his siblings prepared him for caring for an adult child with the same illness. Professionally, he has a Ph.D. in electrical engineering, worked as the director of engineering at a small company making security cameras, and loves the outdoors, animals, and maintaining childlike joy. He is now retired and enjoys simple things like sitting on the backyard patio with the cats and playing handball with his friends. This is some of his wisdom.

Q: Most parents feel a sense of guilt and shame when their child is diagnosed with schizophrenia. The symptoms appear unmanageable, and the family can be left in a crisis, unsure about what resources and help are available. Mothers and fathers of adult children with schizophrenia report that they wonder what they've done wrong and how they can immediately push their child into recovery. How can you relieve the sense of guilt and shame, and the belief that the new diagnosis reflects poor parenting skills? The children can also blame their parents for their suffering in the beginning. How does a parent relieve the guilt and shame they feel both personally and from their child?

A: First, I advise parents to recognize the disorder as a disorder and not the person, just like any physical problem the child might have. Seek out psychiatric help since many symptoms can at least be partially relieved with medication. Investigate what the National Alliance on Mental Illness can offer in terms of support for those not affected.

It’s best to understand that this will probably be a lifelong struggle and that it will not go away. Accepting that as a parent is the first step. Get to a place where you know there should be no guilt or shame in helping anyone with a disease, especially a chronic one that is little understood. Children can be difficult as teenagers even without the disorder, but remember that the brain is not fully developed until around 25 years old, so there is going to be quite a bit of chaos until the child is older. This is normal, and the best response is to stay calm and try to deal with the immediate problems intellectually without getting too emotional and looking for reasons and blame. Punishment is not helpful. Understanding and care are helpful.

Q: Many parents wish to rush their children into recovery immediately upon diagnosis. But oftentimes, those who are diagnosed must take significant amounts of time to even accept that they have a disorder. What do you think is the best strategy for approaching a child who is not ready to take charge of their recovery? If they are not willing to accept the disorder, what is the attitude a parent should begin with when their child is newly diagnosed with a psychotic disorder?

A: I would try to emphasize that they have a disorder and will likely need medication, but specifically elaborate that they are experiencing a disease just like many other disabled people, and just because they have schizophrenia, it doesn’t warrant a worse stigma. Schizophrenia is a disease, like diabetes, which has life-threatening consequences when not managed properly. But one has stigma and the other doesn’t. Try to reduce that stigma within the family. Having a safe place within their immediate family helps to prepare them to face the reality of society. They will likely reject this explanation, but it has to be a constant, gentle reminder, not blameful or forceful. This repeated process of reminding them of the reality while accepting their negative reactions is key for them to grow, because it is a process that will have to be worked with over time. I’ve found being matter-of-fact and supportive in a consistent way, even through the extreme times, has worked the best.

Also, remember that even if they take medication, they will often stop and may need to be placed in a psychiatric facility for their safety and yours. This is a normal part of recovery. This is usually temporary, but will probably repeat several times until they start to accept that they must take medication for their disorder or disease—whichever [term] resonates with them the most. Internalize that there is no blame or shame for a health problem, but know sometimes the behavior is too disruptive to be tolerated. It is OK to get an evaluation of the person and possibly have them be hospitalized in a psychiatric ward until medicine stabilizes them. After they get out, it is helpful to assist them with remembering and taking the medication in a calm and caring way because you understand this is what helps them (and you).

Q: A diagnosis of schizophrenia will likely stay with an adult for the rest of their lives. But as many advocates demonstrate, recovery can result in restorative outcomes. Regardless of what direction the adult chooses to take, their lives are changed permanently, and parents now have a different relationship to their child. How can parents best support their adult children living with this disorder? Should they give ultimatums to pursue recovery? What is a long-term attitude and strategy to have towards their child?

A: There is no such thing as an ultimatum that will help. The person will eventually recover to an extent that they are stable but not someone without the disorder. We do not expect a person without a leg to regrow a leg, so the same attitude must prevail. They can get by with whatever aids help, but they won't be the same as other people. I don’t use the term "normal" because that is derogatory for someone in their situation. Recognize that, in the long term, you yourself as the parent will not be around forever, and they will need to be in a stable environment. Planning ahead is essential. If it is possible to get them in an assisted facility, that is great, but many times that may not be possible. Do try to get whatever government assistance is available and have them declared disabled if at all possible. This opens up government support that enables them to have income and medical support at low cost.

Q: How have you maintained hope throughout your own child's recovery? What specific strategies have helped? What strategies do not help, in your opinion? And what would worsen the outcomes for the relationship between the parent and child?

A: Never blame the child. Be patient and as calm as possible, even though it can be very difficult. Try reasoning with them. This might not work if they are in psychosis, but trying to reason after the episode is better is key. Keep emphasizing facts—often they do not know they are delusional, and it is helpful to remind them of what reality is. Changes might seem slow, but over time they will get to a more stable state even if still having problems. This will probably take as much as 10 years before seeing some real stability. Don't blame them for having a disease. A lot of people get various chronic diseases and live with them with help and medications. Explain this to them and give them examples of physical situations that have similar needs. Also try to point out people with mental problems who still lead fulfilling lives within their limitations. It is very possible to lead a fulfilling life when there is a partnership and intentional relationship between the child and the support team.
